THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Austronesian Languages: From Taiwan Across Half the Globe’s Oceans

Prior to 1500 CE, Austronesian was the single widest geographic language family on Earth, uniting over 1,200 languages across 200 degrees of longitude—from Malagasy off Mozambique across Malay, Javanese, Tagalog, and Chamorro to Hawaiian, Samoan, Te Reo Māori, and Rapa Nui.

Demonstrates Taiwan’s deep linguistic branching and tracks Lapita–Polynesian pauses and pulses across Island Southeast Asia and the Pacific.

Ten subgroups, one outrigger revolution

Nine of the top-level phylogenetic branches of Austronesian belong solely to Formosan Indigenous languages of Taiwan, while all ~1,200 languages across Southeast Asia, Madagascar, and the entire Pacific sit inside a single branch—Malayo-Polynesian—demonstrating Taiwan’s role as the deep geographic point of origin. [1] [2]

Computational trees show crisp expansion pulses matched directly with sailing technology pauses: an initial 1,000-year dwell in Taiwan, rapid Philippines-to-Bismarck voyaging carrying Lapita dentate pottery, and a later pulse across central Polynesia after double-hulled waka refinement. [1] [3]

Borrowed crops, sailing vocabularies, and navigation

Reconstructed Proto-Malayo-Polynesian terms for double-outrigger booms, woven sails, breadfruit, taro, sugarcane, and stone fishhooks demonstrate how maritime voyaging technology evolved continuously alongside ancestral Island Southeast Asian root vocabulary. [1] [2]

Indian Ocean to Rapa Nui literary and oral reach

Austronesian communities carried Southeast Asian musical instruments, rice terraced techniques, and oral genealogical navigation across half the planet—creating Kawi Old Javanese literature on Java alongside chants guiding double-hulled waka across Hawaii, Tahiti, Aotearoa, and Rapa Nui. [4] [2]
